# Observation models and simulated data

## Learning goals

Every earlier chapter built a *process model*: a set of rules that generate the
latent trajectory of an epidemic. Data, however, are never the latent process.
They are noisy, incomplete counts produced by surveillance systems. This chapter
separates the two ideas explicitly and shows how to attach an **observation
model** to a deterministic SIR process so that we can simulate realistic case
reports. After working through it you should be able to

- distinguish a process model from an observation model and explain why the
  distinction matters for inference (Chapters 8 and 9);
- derive daily incidence from a cumulative-infection state and express it as the
  mean of a count distribution;
- implement Poisson and negative-binomial observation models in Julia with
  reproducible random streams; and
- reason about reporting fraction, overdispersion, and the limits of the
  independence assumptions baked into these models.

## Model assumptions and classification

The process model is the standard homogeneously mixing SIR model of
@kermack1927, augmented with a cumulative-incidence state $C$. We reuse the
baseline course scenario throughout: $S(0)=990$, $I(0)=10$, $R(0)=0$,
$N=1000$, contact rate $c=10$, transmission probability $\beta=0.05$, and
recovery rate $\gamma=0.25$, giving a basic reproduction number
$R_0 = \beta c / \gamma = 2$.

| Aspect | Process model | Observation model |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Determinism | deterministic | stochastic |
| Time | continuous | discrete (daily) |
| State | continuous ($S,I,R,C \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$) | discrete counts ($Y_t \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$) |
| Representation | population densities | reported cases |

The observation model rests on three assumptions. First, only *new* infections
generate case reports, so the relevant signal is incidence, not prevalence.
Second, each latent case is reported independently with probability $\rho$ (the
reporting fraction). Third, conditional on the latent incidence, the counts on
different days are independent. The first two assumptions justify a Poisson
count; relaxing the independence of individual reports motivates the
negative-binomial extension.

## Equations

The process model integrates

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}S}{\mathrm{d}t} &= -\beta c \frac{S I}{N}, &
\frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} &= \beta c \frac{S I}{N} - \gamma I, \\[2pt]
\frac{\mathrm{d}R}{\mathrm{d}t} &= \gamma I, &
\frac{\mathrm{d}C}{\mathrm{d}t} &= \beta c \frac{S I}{N},
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-sir-cumulative}

where $C(t)$ accumulates infections but never decreases. The **latent
incidence** over day $t$ is the increment of $C$,

$$
x_t = C(t) - C(t-1) = \int_{t-1}^{t} \beta c \frac{S(\tau) I(\tau)}{N}\,\mathrm{d}\tau .
$$ {#eq-incidence}

The Poisson observation model assumes each expected report equals the reported
fraction of latent incidence,

$$
Y_t \mid x_t \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\rho\, x_t), \qquad
\mathbb{E}[Y_t] = \operatorname{Var}[Y_t] = \rho\, x_t .
$$ {#eq-poisson}

Poisson counts are *equidispersed*: the variance equals the mean. Real
surveillance data are usually **overdispersed**. The negative-binomial model
adds a dispersion parameter $r>0$,

$$
Y_t \mid x_t \sim \operatorname{NegBin}\!\big(r, \tfrac{r}{r + \rho x_t}\big),
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[Y_t] = \rho x_t, \qquad
\operatorname{Var}[Y_t] = \rho x_t + \frac{(\rho x_t)^2}{r},
$$ {#eq-negbin}

so the variance exceeds the mean by $(\rho x_t)^2 / r$, and the Poisson model is
recovered as $r \to \infty$.

## Julia implementation

The process kernel `sir_cumulative_ode!` and the reproducible data generator
`synthetic_incidence` are provided by the course package `EpiModelingCourse`,
so the same code backs the chapter, its slides, and the companion notebook. We
solve the process model with [OrdinaryDiffEq.jl](https://docs.sciml.ai/OrdinaryDiffEq/stable/),
draw observations with [Distributions.jl](https://juliastats.org/Distributions.jl/stable/),
and keep randomness reproducible with
[StableRNGs.jl](https://github.com/JuliaRandom/StableRNGs.jl).

```{julia}
#| label: setup
#| output: false
using EpiModelingCourse
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using DelayDiffEq
using DiffEqCallbacks
using Distributions
using StableRNGs
using CairoMakie

CairoMakie.activate!(type = "png")
set_theme!(course_theme())
palette = course_palette()
```

### The latent process

We integrate @eq-sir-cumulative over 40 days with the baseline parameters and
extract daily incidence by differencing $C$ (Method 1). Because the only exit
from $S$ is infection, cumulative incidence must equal susceptible depletion,
$C(t) = S(0) - S(t)$, which we will use as a validation check.

```{julia}
#| label: process
u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0, 0.0]      # S, I, R, C
p = BASELINE_PARAMETERS            # β = 0.05, c = 10, γ = 0.25, N = 1000
tspan = (0.0, 40.0)
obstimes = 1.0:1.0:40.0

prob = ODEProblem(sir_cumulative_ode!, u0, tspan, p)
sol = solve(prob, Tsit5(); saveat = 1.0, abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10)

cumulative = Array(sol)[4, :]
incidence = cumulative[2:end] .- cumulative[1:(end - 1)]   # latent xₜ
```

### Poisson and negative-binomial observations

With the latent incidence in hand, the observation model is just a draw from a
count distribution. We use a full reporting fraction ($\rho = 1$) here so that
the observation noise, rather than under-reporting, is isolated. Each
observation model gets its own `StableRNG` so the streams are independent and
reproducible.

```{julia}
#| label: observations
reporting_fraction = 1.0
expected = reporting_fraction .* incidence

poisson_obs = rand.(StableRNG(20240607), Poisson.(expected))

# NegativeBinomial(r, p) with mean μ uses p = r / (r + μ); r sets dispersion.
dispersion = 10.0
nb(μ, r) = NegativeBinomial(r, r / (r + μ))
negbin_rng = StableRNG(20240608)
negbin_obs = [rand(negbin_rng, nb(μ, dispersion)) for μ in expected]

(mean_poisson = mean(poisson_obs), var_poisson = var(poisson_obs),
 mean_negbin = mean(negbin_obs), var_negbin = var(negbin_obs))
```

The sample variance of the Poisson draws tracks their mean, while the
negative-binomial draws are visibly overdispersed, exactly as @eq-poisson and
@eq-negbin predict.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-observations
#| fig-cap: "Latent daily incidence (line) with one realisation of Poisson (left) and overdispersed negative-binomial (right) case reports. Both share the same latent mean; the negative-binomial scatter is wider."
fig = Figure(size = (900, 380))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "Time (days)", ylabel = "New cases per day",
    title = "Poisson observations")
barplot!(ax1, obstimes, poisson_obs; color = (palette.incidence, 0.5))
lines!(ax1, obstimes, incidence; color = palette.infected, linewidth = 3,
    label = "Latent incidence")
axislegend(ax1; position = :rt)

ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; xlabel = "Time (days)", ylabel = "New cases per day",
    title = "Negative-binomial observations (r = $(Int(dispersion)))")
barplot!(ax2, obstimes, negbin_obs; color = (palette.incidence, 0.5))
lines!(ax2, obstimes, incidence; color = palette.infected, linewidth = 3)
fig
```

### Alternative ways to obtain daily incidence

Differencing the cumulative state (Method 1) is the most robust route, but two
other constructions appear in practice. A [PresetTimeCallback](https://docs.sciml.ai/DiffEqCallbacks/stable/)
can reset $C$ to zero at each observation time so that the saved value *is* the
daily increment (Method 2). A delay differential equation solved with
[DelayDiffEq.jl](https://github.com/SciML/DelayDiffEq.jl) can track a sliding
one-day window directly (Method 3). We implement both to compare them against
Method 1.

```{julia}
#| label: alt-methods
# Method 2: reset the cumulative counter at each observation time.
reset_C!(integrator) = integrator.u[4] = 0.0
cb = PresetTimeCallback(collect(obstimes), reset_C!)
sol_cb = solve(prob, Tsit5(); saveat = 1.0, callback = cb,
    abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10)
incidence_cb = sol_cb(obstimes)[4, :]

# Method 3: a sliding-window delay differential equation for daily incidence.
function sir_window_dde!(du, u, h, p, t)
    S, I, R, C = u
    N = p.N
    infection = p.β * p.c * S * I / N
    recovery = p.γ * I
    past = h(p, t - 1.0)          # state one day earlier
    past_infection = p.β * p.c * past[1] * past[2] / N
    du[1] = -infection
    du[2] = infection - recovery
    du[3] = recovery
    du[4] = infection - past_infection
    return nothing
end
history(p, t) = zeros(4)
prob_dde = DDEProblem(sir_window_dde!, u0, history, tspan, p; constant_lags = [1.0])
sol_dde = solve(prob_dde, MethodOfSteps(Tsit5()))
incidence_dde = sol_dde(obstimes)[4, :]

(method2_max_gap = maximum(abs.(incidence_cb .- incidence)),
 method3_max_gap = maximum(abs.(incidence_dde .- incidence)))
```

Method 2 agrees with Method 1 to solver tolerance. Method 3 differs by roughly
one case near the epidemic peak: the delayed state is interpolated rather than
differenced, so it is a genuinely different (though closely related) quantity.
For downstream inference we therefore prefer Method 1.

## Validation

We check three structural properties. First, conservation: cumulative incidence
must equal susceptible depletion. Second, non-negativity: sampled counts are
never negative. Third, the law of large numbers: averaging many independent
Poisson realisations must converge to the latent mean @eq-poisson.

```{julia}
#| label: validation
S = Array(sol)[1, :]
conservation_error = maximum(abs.(cumulative .- (990.0 .- S)))

replicates = [rand.(StableRNG(seed), Poisson.(expected)) for seed in 1:2000]
mc_mean = reduce(+, replicates) ./ length(replicates)
lln_error = maximum(abs.(mc_mean .- expected))

(conservation_error = conservation_error,
 counts_nonnegative = all(poisson_obs .>= 0) && all(negbin_obs .>= 0),
 lln_error = lln_error)
```

The conservation error sits at the level of the ODE tolerances, all counts are
non-negative, and the Monte Carlo mean of 2000 Poisson realisations reproduces
the latent incidence to within a fraction of a case.

## Interpretation and limitations

The observation model is deliberately simple, and each assumption is a modelling
choice a practitioner must defend. Because $\rho$ and the transmission rate both
scale the expected count, a *single* incidence series cannot separate a small
epidemic reported fully from a large epidemic reported partially — an
identifiability problem revisited in the sensitivity and identifiability
chapter.
The Poisson model forces variance to equal the mean, so it understates
uncertainty whenever reporting is clustered, batched, or driven by super-
spreading; the negative-binomial model in @eq-negbin is the usual remedy, at the
cost of one extra parameter. We also assumed instantaneous reporting: real
systems impose delays between infection and notification, which the delay
formulation of Method 3 hints at but does not fully capture. Finally,
conditional independence across days ignores weekday reporting artefacts and
autocorrelated reporting effort. These simulated datasets are nonetheless the
raw material for the inference chapters that follow: Chapter 8 estimates
parameters from them by maximum likelihood, and Chapter 9 does so with Bayesian
methods.

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 {#ch07-ex1}

Using the baseline scenario and Method 1, generate case reports under a partial
reporting fraction $\rho = 0.4$ with the Poisson observation model. Plot the
latent incidence and the reported counts on the same axes, and compute the total
number of latent versus reported cases over the 40 days. Explain why the reported
peak looks like a smaller epidemic and why $\rho$ and $\beta$ cannot be
distinguished from the reported series alone.

### Exercise 2 {#ch07-ex2}

Fix the mean of the negative-binomial observation model to the latent incidence
and vary the dispersion parameter over $r \in \{1, 5, 50\}$. For each value,
draw 1000 replicate time series and estimate the ratio of the sample variance to
the sample mean at the epidemic peak. Confirm numerically that the ratio
approaches 1 as $r$ grows, connecting your result to the variance formula in
@eq-negbin.
